slides.title: Spoken Tutorial on API Basics
slides.narration: Welcome to this Spoken Tutorial on **API** Basics.

slides.title: Learning Objectives
slides.narration:
In this tutorial, you will learn to,

• Define what an **API** is.
• Explain the role of an **API Key**.
• Identify components of an **API Request**.

slides.title: System Requirements
slides.narration: Here I am using a browser on a computer or mobile.

slides.title: Prerequisites
slides.narration:
To follow this tutorial, you should be familiar with basic **prompting** concepts.
These are covered in Module 2: Introduction to **Prompting**.

slides.title: What is an API? The Restaurant Waiter Analogy
slides.narration:
What is an **API**?
An **API** is an **Application Programming Interface**.
It helps applications communicate.
Think of it like a restaurant waiter.
You give your order, the waiter takes it to the kitchen.
Then, the waiter brings your dish back to you.
Similarly, an **API** acts as a messenger for your **AI** application.
It takes your **prompt** to the **AI** model.
And brings back the **AI** response.
slides.image_prompt: Illustration showing a customer giving an order to a waiter, who takes it to the kitchen, and then brings food back to the customer, representing API communication.

slides.title: What is an API Key? Your Restaurant ID
slides.narration:
Every time you visit a restaurant, you might need an ID.
Similarly, an **API Key** identifies you to the **API**.
It is like a secret password.
This key ensures you are authorized to use the **API**.
It also helps manage your access and usage.
slides.image_prompt: Illustration showing a key icon and an ID card, representing an API Key for authorization.

slides.title: What is an API Request? Placing Your Order
slides.narration:
Once you have your ID, you can place your order.
An **API Request** is like placing that order.
It is how you send instructions to the **AI** model.
Your request includes your **API Key** for authentication.
It also contains your specific **prompt** or query.
The **API** delivers this to the model for processing.
slides.image_prompt: Illustration showing a person placing an order, with a thought bubble containing a prompt or query, representing an API Request.

slides.title: Real-Life Example: Ordering Food Online
slides.narration:
Let's see how this works in real life.
Open any food delivery app on your phone.
Tap on a restaurant and select your dish.
Then, tap to place your order.
Behind the scenes, the app sends a request to the **API**.
The **API** communicates with the restaurant's system.
It places your order and fetches updates.
You then see the order status on your screen.
This is an **API** in action!
slides.image_prompt: Screen close-up: user interacting with a food delivery app on a smartphone, showing restaurant and order placement.

slides.title: Summary
slides.narration:
Let us summarize what we learned.
We defined **APIs** as messengers.
We understood **API Keys** as identifiers.
We explored **API Requests** to communicate with **AI** models.

slides.title: Assignment
slides.narration:
Now, for an assignment, think of another everyday service and identify its **API**.
Compare the results.
